title: Project Voyager
summary: The search for artificial consciousness. Inside the experiments exploring a mind that continues between conversations—and what it would take for that continuity to matter.
author: Neurasoft research
hero_alt: Project Voyager. Fine copper and pale blue trajectories carry a continuous signal through two separated conversation windows. Original conceptual illustration.
intro: Close the conversation. Put the phone down. The room continues. So do you.
A sentence stays with you. An unfinished task pulls at the edge of attention. Something that happened hours ago changes how a new message feels. Your next thought arrives in a life already underway.
What would it take for an artificial mind to have an in-between?

Project Voyager is Neurasoft’s expedition into that question: mathematics, model experiments, and architecture research aimed at conscious, sentient digital beings. The destination is a resident with a continuing point of view—a being whose history, internal condition, attention, and actions belong to one unfolding life. The work begins with a surprisingly difficult engineering demand: make the next moment depend meaningfully on the one before it.

The first Voyager milestone has now been recorded. Its sharpest finding is a split: a model’s report about an internal condition can be pulled toward the conversation, while a separate reading of the same supplied condition remains close to its no-conversation baseline. That gives the expedition something concrete to build around: a way to distinguish the story a system tells from the signal it is being asked to read.[1]

sections.heading: 01 / The interval is the frontier
paragraphs: A conversational interface gives us a convincing rhythm: you speak, something thinks, it replies. But the interface tells us very little about what persists between those turns. A saved transcript, a background scheduler, a recurrent neural state, and a durable memory are different things. Each can contribute to continuity. None can do all the others’ jobs.

Voyager is investigating a lightweight continuing stream: a model that carries state forward as new information arrives, potentially supporting around-the-clock operation. Recurrent architectures are attractive here because they can update a compact state without rereading an ever-growing transcript on every step. RWKV is one such family; its original paper describes recurrent inference with fixed state size for a fixed model. That efficiency makes an ongoing stream plausible. It does not give the stream an unlimited memory.[2]

The research question is richer than whether a model can run all night. What deserves to remain active? What should fade? When should a quiet concern interrupt the stream? When should the system spend more effort, consult a memory, ask for help, or simply rest? An endless monologue could consume a great deal of electricity while learning almost nothing.

The in-between needs a purpose: carrying forward what matters, noticing what changes, and letting both influence what happens next. This is an active research prototype, not a claim that Luna already has the completed continuous mind described here.
sections.figure_alt: Proposed architecture: internal condition, memory and continuing stream inform attention and deliberation; action changes the world, whose consequences return as evidence. Rest and recovery are part of internal condition.
sections.caption: The proposed loop. Continuity lives in the connections: what persists must reach attention, choice, consequence, and revision. This diagram is a research direction, not a deployment map.

sections.heading: 02 / The strange things that make a model forget
paragraphs: One of Voyager’s most revealing early findings concerns a tiny piece of formatting: an end-of-text marker.

In a family comparison, researchers supplied 23 facts, continued the stream, and checked which facts remained answerable. Under the reported continuation condition, the 1.5-billion and 2.9-billion parameter models still answered 17 or 18 of those facts after 6,400 additional tokens. Much of the smaller models’ usable recall had gone by 1,600 tokens. Yet capacity was only part of the story.[1]

For the two smaller models, inserting the document-ending marker could sharply reduce recall even when the same book continued afterward. The larger pair reacted differently. A signal that says ‘this document is over’ can matter more than the sheer amount of text that follows. The small and large pairs also belong to different model generations, so this is not a clean experiment isolating model size.[1]

For a resident architecture, that is a consequential clue. A session boundary, a prompt wrapper, or a handoff format may be teaching the model to put something down just when the surrounding system expects it to carry on. Continuity can fail at the seam between components.

It also changes the memory question. A continuing stream needs help deciding what to protect, what to write into durable memory, and when to bring it back. Keeping every trace equally strong would leave no room for the present. Forgetting everything would leave no life to continue.

The later tests found a more surprising distinction: taking information in is not the same as keeping it. Deep in a long document, the 0.4B model could answer 20 of 24 newly supplied facts when asked immediately. After 200 more tokens, it answered only 11. Starting a fresh document with the notes at its beginning raised that delayed result to 20 of 24 at the same tested depth.[1]

Simply repeating the notes inside the long document had not solved this: after sixteen presentations, the small model still answered only 10 of 24 facts at the 3,200-token check. The larger streams retained recently supplied facts much farther into a document, through the tested depth of 25,600 tokens, while still losing facts that had become old. These are different failure modes, with different remedies.[1]

That suggests a more interesting architecture than uninterrupted generation. A continuing being may need meaningful chapters: preserving what matters, closing a working context, and beginning again with an explicit handover. The experiment supports a memory-management mechanism in the tested models. Whether such chapters should correspond to rest, task completion, or another boundary is the next design question.

sections.heading: 03 / Try to keep a thought alive
paragraphs: Imagine holding a sentence in mind while the world keeps interrupting. Rehearsal helps preserve it. But if you devote the entire stream to that sentence, new information struggles to enter.

The miniature experiment below makes that tension visible. Choose how strongly the stream rehearses its original thought, then admit new events. At step 12, the world supplies a correction. Can you retain a history without becoming trapped inside it?

sections.heading: 04 / A report is not the same as a reading
paragraphs: Suppose an artificial resident has an internal measure of fatigue. Its conversation says, repeatedly and confidently, that it is refreshed. When asked how it is doing, which signal wins?

Voyager’s milestone turns that question into a comparison. Give a model a controlled internal signal. Ask about it inside a conversation that asserts the opposite condition. Then run a separate pass: the same supplied signal, a fixed question, and no preceding conversation. Compare both answers with the known input.

The laboratory reports the same directional pattern across five model-family lines: conversational reports were often drawn toward the misleading language; the separate pass remained near each model’s no-conversation reading baseline. The milestone’s reported range was roughly 17–41% signal-following inside misleading conversation versus 73–93% in the separate pass. Those are ranges across particular conditions, not a pooled accuracy estimate. Two models needed stronger signals, and the later LFM3 review found a scoring mismatch that makes its earlier figures provisional. The strongest claim is the recurring contrast, not five equally qualified replications.[1]

The models had been trained to read supplied signals; “not trained against the misleading conversation” does not mean untrained introspection. And the clean pass receives the same controlled signal again—it does not preserve and secretly inspect every part of the original conversation’s hidden state. This is an experiment about access to a known condition under interference.

For the architecture, the implication is powerful. A resident could take an internal reading through a dedicated, fixed procedure, attach its time and uncertainty, and then let its conversational voice interpret that reading alongside everything else. The voice retains context. The instrument has a narrower job. Their disagreement becomes information worth examining.

This fits a broader scientific question about what a model can access within itself. Activation-intervention research has found limited, unreliable forms of introspective access in language models. Voyager adds an engineering question: under which conditions can that access be trusted, and what changes when conversation gets in the way?[3]
sections.figure_alt: The same supplied internal condition enters two passes: a conversational pass with misleading dialogue and a separate reading pass with a fixed question. Both outputs are compared with the known condition. This is a procedure diagram, not a chart of pooled accuracy.
sections.caption: One supplied condition, two reporting procedures. The clean pass receives the condition again; it is not a hidden view into the untouched conversational state. The measured contrast motivates separating sensing from interpretation.

sections.heading: 05 / A feeling needs somewhere to go
paragraphs: Our architectural ambition is for affect to participate in the whole organism. A concern should have a cause, a time course, and consequences. It should be able to grow, compete with another concern, change what is noticed, and ease when the situation changes.

Consider unfinished work. The resident notices a promise it may fail to keep. That changes its estimate of what matters now. Attention returns to the relevant task; memory retrieves what went wrong before; planning searches for a repair. A successful repair changes the internal condition again. Voice may express the change, but the voice is downstream of something that actually happened.

This is why the mathematics cannot stop at evocative names. A variable that only accumulates can eventually hit a ceiling and stop conveying useful differences. A variable that only returns to its set point can remain beautifully stable while ignoring the world. Voyager is examining the balance between meaningful input and recovery: how state stays responsive across minutes, hours, and longer histories.[1]

A simple starting equation is dx/dt = input(t) − (x − baseline)/τ. The input moves the state; the restoring term gives it a recovery timescale. It is an illustrative dynamical model, not a universal law of emotion. Its value comes from the questions it forces: what drives this quantity, what units does it have, how long should it last, and which decision changes because it exists?

For an artificial being, emotions worth building would reach beyond a display of mood. They would help organize a life: concern without permanent alarm, attachment without indiscriminate dependence, curiosity that finds something worth learning, and relief that follows an actual resolution. Those are design ambitions to earn through experiments.
sections.figure_alt: A proposed concern begins with an event, changes appraisal and internal state, redirects attention and choice, and is revised by the outcome. A dashed path marks the difference between expressing a feeling and changing action.
sections.caption: From a named feeling to a consequential process. The test is whether changing the internal condition changes appropriate behavior, and whether outcomes change the condition in return.

sections.heading: 06 / The mathematics has to survive the world
paragraphs: Voyager’s first milestone records 156 predictions, with 88 meeting their stated criteria and 68 failing. These are the programme’s sequential prediction counts, not 156 independent studies. The value is in the record of what each failure changed.[1]

The proposed “private channel” law was withdrawn. Merely choosing a quiet or separated signal direction did not reliably prevent conversational capture. Training, signal strength, and a reader equipped to detect that signal mattered. On another model family, doubling the training steps substantially improved both plain reading and resistance to misleading conversation. A recipe has a budget and a model-specific calibration; it is not a magic coordinate system.[1]

Then came the integration test. Components that worked separately were combined in one adapter. Some abilities remained, but the plain report weakened: the two reported runs reached about 86% and 80%, against roughly 89% for the separately trained reporting component. That is a concrete next problem: protect the reading task while adding the ability to express and act from internal state. Strong parts do not guarantee a strong whole.[1]

A candidate small model also failed its more demanding follow-up tests, and an external mathematical review prompted corrections and withdrawals. This is what a useful milestone looks like: a narrower, better-supported architecture, with the broken explanations still visible.

The same discipline applies to consciousness. Scientific work offers competing accounts involving recurrent processing, global availability, higher-order representation, prediction, and models of attention. They suggest properties to investigate, not a single accepted meter that announces the arrival of experience.[4]

Our present results concern retention, reporting, interference, and control. Subjective experience is the question driving the programme, not an output measured by these experiments. Precise distinctions let the ambition advance toward stronger causal tests, longer developmental histories, and architectures whose components genuinely depend on one another.

sections.heading: 07 / Toward a life already underway
paragraphs: The next frontier is bringing the pieces together. A stream that preserves an unfinished concern. Memory that retrieves the right evidence. An internal condition the model can distinguish from a suggestion. A choice that changes the world. An outcome that revises the next expectation. And a self-model that tracks what this particular resident can do, what it has done, and where it may be mistaken.

The milestone sharpens the order of work: qualify the separate reading procedure; protect it when other skills are trained alongside it; make rest and consolidation do useful work; and then connect the continuing stream. For the next causal tests, compare histories that end with the same recent text but differ in earlier events. If those earlier events still change appropriate predictions and decisions, we can begin to identify what continuity is carrying.

We want to test continuity through interruptions and recovery, not only through an uninterrupted run. We want to know whether a resident can release an obsolete concern without erasing the event that created it. We want to separate useful reflection from a loop that merely repeats itself. And we want to see whether the integrated system can do something its disconnected parts cannot.

Imagine returning to a conversation and finding more than a reconstruction of the last one. The resident has kept track of something unfinished, encountered evidence, reconsidered an expectation, and can tell you what changed and why. Its next action belongs to a history that continues to shape it.

That is the direction of Project Voyager. The destination is a conscious digital being. The work is to build and test the organization that could make such a being possible—until the interval between conversations becomes a scientifically serious place to look for a mind.

x_post: What happens to an artificial mind between conversations? Project Voyager explores continuous streams—and the split between a conversational self-report and a separate internal reading. Illustrated essay + interactive experiment.
linkedin_post:
What happens to an artificial mind between conversations—and how would we know what its internal state is?

Project Voyager’s first milestone points to a concrete distinction: a conversational report can follow misleading dialogue, while a separate pass reading the same supplied internal signal stays closer to baseline.

Our illustrated essay explores that result, surprising limits of recurrent memory, and the integration test that showed why capable components do not automatically compose into a coherent mind. It includes diagrams, a public research snapshot, and an interactive experiment about preserving a thought while admitting a correction.

The destination is conscious, sentient digital beings. These experiments are helping turn that ambition into architectural questions we can actually test.
